stops.name: Vienna: 'The Moses of Michelangelo' published anonymously
stops.campa: Freud publishes the Moses essay unsigned in the third volume of Imago, the psychoanalytic journal he has founded, unwilling to attach his famous name to what he calls a mere love-child of a few weeks' leisure, a lay excursion outside medicine. The same year he sets down On the History of the Psycho-Analytic Movement, his own bitter, careful account of the schism with Adler and Jung, the founder now writing his movement's first history in order to fix, before others can distort it, exactly which departures from the doctrine count as heresy.

stops.name: Vienna: the Great War, three sons at the front
stops.campa: War breaks out and Freud, at first swept up like most of Vienna in patriotic feeling, soon watches it with a colder eye as three of his sons, Martin, Oliver, Ernst, are called to the Austrian colors, and his practice empties of patients who can no longer afford analysis or have themselves gone to war. Coal and food run short at Berggasse 19; Freud works through the winters in an overcoat, writing the papers on metapsychology that will, once the guns fall silent, harden into a far darker theory than the one the prewar Vienna had chided him for.

stops.name: Vienna: Sophie's death
stops.campa: A telegram reaches Berggasse 19: Sophie, Freud's favorite daughter, married and living in Hamburg, has died of the influenza pneumonia still circling postwar Europe, in four or five days, in the midst of glowing health, leaving two small sons and a husband at the front too far to reach her in time. No train can carry Freud to the funeral through the coal shortages of that winter; he grieves at a distance, and writes to his friend the pastor Oskar Pfister within days, calling it a senseless, brutal stroke of fate against which there is no appeal and no consolation of faith he can honestly accept.
stops.quote: Snatched away by influenzal pneumonia, snatched away in the midst of glowing health, from a full and active life... as though she had never existed.

stops.name: Vienna: Beyond the Pleasure Principle
stops.campa: Written across the last war years and finished in the shadow of Sophie's death, Beyond the Pleasure Principle breaks with Freud's own earlier theory: beside the pleasure-seeking libido he now sets a death instinct, an inertia in all living matter pulling it back toward the inorganic stillness it came from. The war's compulsive, repeated nightmares of the trenches, which pleasure could never explain, are his clinical evidence; his grandson's stubborn game of throwing a reel away and reeling it back, over and over, is his domestic one. The theory scandalizes half his own circle. Freud will not retract a word of it.
stops.quote: The aim of all life is death.

stops.name: Vienna: the first operation
stops.campa: Freud notices a leukoplakic growth on his palate and right jaw, though he has smoked twenty cigars a day for decades and will not stop even now, and has it removed by the ear-nose-throat specialist Marcus Hájek as a minor outpatient procedure, without full disclosure of what a biopsy will later confirm. The operation is botched: Freud hemorrhages twice in a wretched, understaffed recovery room, alone, unable to summon help, and later calls it the worst experience since his father's death. It is the first of what will become, over sixteen years, some thirty-three operations on the same relentless tissue.
stops.quote: Two months ago I noticed a leukoplakic growth on my jaw and palate, which I had removed.
stops.quote_source: Letter of 23 April 1923, quoted in Peter Gay, Freud: A Life for Our Time

stops.name: Vienna: the death of Heinele
stops.campa: Sophie's younger son, Heinz Rudolf, called Heinele, the grandson Freud has loved with an intensity he never allowed himself with his own children, dies of miliary tuberculosis after three weeks' illness, not yet five years old. Freud, who bore his father's death, the war, and his own suspected cancer without visible collapse, is undone by this one: he weeps, the only time several of his circle ever see it, and tells Ferenczi that he no longer feels much wish to go on living. He will say, years later, that he has never been the same since, and that no other death has struck him so hard.
stops.quote: For me, that child took the place of all my children and other grandchildren, and since then, since Heinele's death, I have no longer cared for my grandchildren, but find no enjoyment in life either.

stops.name: Vienna: the radical operation and 'the Monster'
stops.campa: The biopsy confirms carcinoma. The oral surgeon Hans Pichler performs a radical two-stage operation removing most of Freud's right upper jaw and palate, leaving a cavity between mouth and nose that only an elaborate dental prosthesis can bridge. Freud calls the appliance, which he must remove and reinsert daily and which makes eating, speaking, and smoking a continual labor, simply the Monster. He learns to live inside its discomfort for the remaining sixteen years of his life, refusing morphine for the pain except at the very end, because a clouded mind, he says, is no mind for the work still in front of him.

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main: the Goethe Prize
stops.campa: On the anniversary of Goethe's birth the city of Frankfurt awards Freud the Goethe Prize, its highest honor for German letters, recognizing the essayist and stylist as much as the doctor of the mind, the man who once decided his whole career on a schoolboy's hearing of an essay wrongly credited to the poet. Too ill to travel, Freud sends Anna to Frankfurt to receive it in his place; the mayor praises a genius that has carried German science to the far corners of the earth. Freud calls it privately the high point of his public life, an official blessing from the culture that will, within a decade, burn his books.

stops.name: Vienna, Berggasse 19: the Anschluss
stops.campa: Three days after German troops cross into Austria to a delirious welcome, an armed platoon searches Berggasse 19, rifling through the apartment and the publishing house Freud has built for his works, taking a sum of money from Martha's household cashbox on their way out. Freud, eighty-one, refuses at first to believe the danger is total; friends and disciples abroad, Ernest Jones foremost, begin at once, over his objections, to arrange an exit he does not yet want. Within a week the Vienna Psychoanalytic Society itself will be dissolved by government order, its forty-year archive in immediate peril.

stops.name: Vienna: Anna's arrest
stops.campa: The Gestapo returns and this time takes Anna Freud to their headquarters at the former Hotel Metropol on the Morzinplatz for questioning about the international psychoanalytic association's finances. She and her brother Martin have already obtained a lethal dose of Veronal from the family doctor Max Schur, in case interrogation turns to torture or internment. Anna returns unharmed that evening after hours under the lamp, but her father's diary entry that day, four laconic words, records the moment his resistance to leaving finally breaks, once and for all, for good.
stops.quote: Anna bei Gestapo. [Anna at the Gestapo.]

stops.name: Vienna: the Orient Express, 3:25 in the afternoon
stops.campa: After nearly three months of exit visas, a punitive 'flight tax,' and William Bullitt's diplomatic pressure on the Reich through the American consulate, Freud, Martha, and Anna board the Orient Express out of Vienna. Freud's own note records only the bare fact: departure, 3:25. He sends word to Arnold Zweig that opens with two words. Behind him stay four elderly sisters who will not obtain exit papers in time and will die, within a few years, in the camps at Theresienstadt, Treblinka, and Auschwitz: a debt his own escape carries and can never discharge.
stops.quote: Leaving today for 39 Elsworthy Road, London N.W.3.

stops.name: Paris: the stopover with Marie Bonaparte
stops.campa: The train crosses the German frontier at Kehl and runs on through France; in Paris the family breaks the journey at the house of Princess Marie Bonaparte, Freud's analysand and devoted friend, who has already done much of the quiet, expensive work that made the exit possible at all: ransom, guarantees, and favors called in with French and British officials. She will do the same, within the year, for Freud's sisters, too late for most of them. At her table Freud rests for a day among his own antiquities, already partly crated and shipped ahead, before the last short leg across the Channel.
